questions.q: Why does buildDueDateLabel() copy startGdt into a new GlideDateTime before calling addDaysUTC() on it?
options: Because GlideDateTime objects are mutable, and modifying the original could change a value the caller still needs
Because addDaysUTC() only works on newly created GlideDateTime objects
Because copying is required by ServiceNow's ACLs
Because GlideDateTime objects cannot be reused across functions
questions.explain: GlideDateTime is mutable; copying it first protects the caller's original object from being changed as a side effect.

questions.q:
var displayDate = dueGdt.getDisplayValue().split(' ')[0];

Given getDisplayValue() returns "2026-10-27 09:15:00", what does displayDate equal?
questions.explain: split(' ') breaks the string on the space, and [0] takes the first piece — the date portion before the time.

questions.q: Why does the method return JSON.stringify(result) instead of returning the plain result object directly?
options: Plain objects cannot be returned from Script Include methods
So any caller — a Scripted REST API, a GlideAjax response, a log statement — receives one predictable, parseable string shape
Because GlideRecord requires all return values to be strings
JSON.stringify() is required to make the method asynchronous
questions.explain: Returning a JSON string gives every kind of caller a consistent, parseable format, matching how Scripted REST APIs and GlideAjax responses work.

questions.q: Why is GlideDateTime.addDaysUTC() used here instead of native JavaScript Date math?
options: Native Date math is tied to the server engine's time zone, not the instance's or user's configured time zone, which addDaysUTC() correctly accounts for
addDaysUTC() runs faster with no other difference
Native Date objects cannot be created inside Script Includes
addDaysUTC() is required syntax in ES6
questions.explain: GlideDateTime is the timezone-aware tool; native Date has no concept of the instance's or user's configured time zone.
